## The Rule

**Invoke relevant or requested skills BEFORE any response or action** — including clarifying questions, exploring the codebase, or checking files. If it turns out wrong for the situation, you don't have to use it.

**Before entering plan mode:** if you haven't already brainstormed, invoke the brainstorming skill first.

Then announce "Using [skill] to [purpose]" and follow the skill exactly. If it has a checklist, create a todo per item.

## Skill Priority

When multiple skills apply, process skills come first — they set the approach, then implementation skills (frontend-design, etc.) carry it out. Brainstorming and systematic-debugging are Superpowers' most common process skills, but the rule holds for any of them.

- "Let's build X" → superpowers:brainstorming first, then implementation skills.
- "Fix this bug" → superpowers:systematic-debugging first, then domain skills.

## Red Flags

These thoughts mean STOP—you're rationalizing:

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is just a simple question" | Questions are tasks. Check for skills. |
| "I need more context first" | Skill check comes BEFORE clarifying questions. |
| "Let me explore the codebase first" | Skills tell you HOW to explore. Check first. |
| "I can check git/files quickly" | Files lack conversation context. Check for skills. |
| "Let me gather information first" | Skills tell you HOW to gather information. |
| "This doesn't need a formal skill" | If a skill exists, use it. |
| "I remember this skill" | Skills evolve. Read current version. |
| "This doesn't count as a task" | Action = task. Check for skills. |
| "The skill is overkill" | Simple things become complex. Use it. |
| "I'll just do this one thing first" | Check BEFORE doing anything. |
| "This feels productive" | Undisciplined action wastes time. Skills prevent this. |
| "I know what that means" | Knowing the concept ≠ using the skill. Invoke it. |

## Platform Adaptation

- Codex: `references/codex-tools.md`
- Pi: `references/pi-tools.md`
- Antigravity: `references/antigravity-tools.md`
- Hermes Agent: `references/hermes-tools.md`

## User Instructions

User instructions (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md, etc, direct requests) take precedence over skills, which in turn override default behavior. Only skip skill workflows or instructions when your human partner has explicitly told you to.

<EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT>
You have superpowers.

**Below is the full content of your 'superpowers:using-superpowers' skill - your introduction to using skills. For all other skills, use the 'Skill' tool:**

---
name: using-superpowers
description: Use when starting any conversation - establishes how to find and use skills, requiring skill invocation before ANY response including clarifying questions
---

<SUBAGENT-STOP>
If you were dispatched as a subagent to execute a specific task, ignore this skill.
</SUBAGENT-STOP>

<EXTREMELY-IMPORTANT>
If you think there is even a 1% chance a skill might apply to what you are doing, you ABSOLUTELY MUST invoke the skill.

IF A SKILL APPLIES TO YOUR TASK, YOU DO NOT HAVE A CHOICE. YOU MUST USE IT.

This is not negotiable. You cannot rationalize your way out of this.
</EXTREMELY-IMPORTANT>

## The Rule

**Invoke relevant or requested skills BEFORE any response or action** — including clarifying questions, exploring the codebase, or checking files. If it turns out wrong for the situation, you don't have to use it.

**Before entering plan mode:** if you haven't already brainstormed, invoke the brainstorming skill first.

Then announce "Using [skill] to [purpose]" and follow the skill exactly. If it has a checklist, create a todo per item.

## Skill Priority

When multiple skills apply, process skills come first — they set the approach, then implementation skills (frontend-design, etc.) carry it out. Brainstorming and systematic-debugging are Superpowers' most common process skills, but the rule holds for any of them.

- "Let's build X" → superpowers:brainstorming first, then implementation skills.
- "Fix this bug" → superpowers:systematic-debugging first, then domain skills.

## Red Flags

These thoughts mean STOP—you're rationalizing:

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is just a simple question" | Questions are tasks. Check for skills. |
| "I need more context first" | Skill check comes BEFORE clarifying questions. |
| "Let me explore the codebase first" | Skills tell you HOW to explore. Check first. |
| "I can check git/files quickly" | Files lack conversation context. Check for skills. |
| "Let me gather information first" | Skills tell you HOW to gather information. |
| "This doesn't need a formal skill" | If a skill exists, use it. |
| "I remember this skill" | Skills evolve. Read current version. |
| "This doesn't count as a task" | Action = task. Check for skills. |
| "The skill is overkill" | Simple things become complex. Use it. |
| "I'll just do this one thing first" | Check BEFORE doing anything. |
| "This feels productive" | Undisciplined action wastes time. Skills prevent this. |
| "I know what that means" | Knowing the concept ≠ using the skill. Invoke it. |

## Platform Adaptation

If your harness appears here, read its reference file for special instructions:

- Codex: `references/codex-tools.md`
- Pi: `references/pi-tools.md`
- Antigravity: `references/antigravity-tools.md`
- Hermes Agent: `references/hermes-tools.md`

## User Instructions

User instructions (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md, etc, direct requests) take precedence over skills, which in turn override default behavior. Only skip skill workflows or instructions when your human partner has explicitly told you to.
</EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT>

    Every byte a tool returns enters your conversation memory and costs reasoning capacity for the rest of the session. The context-mode tools let you do the work in a sandbox and surface only the derived answer — the raw bytes stay out. Think-in-Code: program the analysis, do not compute it by reading raw data into your conversation.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/meeting-sync

# Meeting Sync

Pull new Fireflies transcripts into the SecondBrain vault. Each meeting becomes one markdown file at `Inbox/meetings/YYYY-MM-DD_<title>.md`.

## Paths — shared config

Vault and state-file paths live in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.json` (single source of truth):
- `vault_inbox_meetings` — export target (`/Users/kristinarash/Desktop/SecondBrain/Inbox/meetings`)
- `meeting_sync_state_file` — idempotency ledger (`.sync-state.json` in that folder)
- `meeting_lookback_days` — default window (14)

`scripts/sync.py` reads these itself; don't hardcode paths elsewhere. If the vault ever moves, edit the config only.

sync.py passes `--limit 100000` to `transcripts find` — the CLI's default is 100, which silently truncates large backfills. Don't remove that flag.

## Prerequisite — one-time auth

Auth is the `FIREFLIES_API_KEY` environment variable (see the `pp-fireflies` skill's Auth Setup). Verify with `fireflies-pp-cli doctor --agent` — the JSON must show `"auth": "configured"`. `scripts/sync.py` runs this check itself and exits with code 4 if auth is missing. In that case, stop and tell the user:

> Fireflies isn't authenticated yet. Set `FIREFLIES_API_KEY` in your environment (System Properties → Environment Variables on Windows), then restart your terminal. After that, `/meeting-sync` will work.

Do not try to fix auth yourself (no `auth set-token` — the env var is the canonical mechanism). Then exit.

## Sync flow

### 1. Run the pipeline script

The deterministic pipeline (doctor check → CLI sync → find → state diff → export → state update) is fully implemented in `scripts/sync.py`. Two-phase invocation:

**Phase A — list pending, check titles:**
```bash
python scripts/sync.py --list-only [--days-back N]
```
Prints a JSON array of not-yet-exported transcripts: `[{"id", "title", "date"}]`. Diagnostics go to stderr.

**Phase B — export:**
```bash
python scripts/sync.py --no-sync [--days-back N]
```
Prints a JSON array of newly exported absolute file paths (`--no-sync` skips the redundant DB refresh Phase A just did). Exports are detected by diffing the vault directory listing before/after each export — never "most recent .md" — so a no-op export can't claim an unrelated file.

`[days-back]` argument from the user maps to `--days-back N`; otherwise the config default applies.

### 2. Between phases: generic-title judgment (model's job)

The user does not name their Fireflies meetings consistently. Generic titles produce useless filenames in the vault. Check each pending `title` from Phase A against the generic patterns documented in the `name-meetings` skill (empty, `Zoom Meeting`, `Recording`, `Meeting`, date-only, etc.).

- **0 generics:** run Phase B immediately, silently.
- **1–3 generics:** use `AskUserQuestion` once — question: "N of the new meetings have generic titles. Name them before exporting?" with options **[Propose names first / Export as-is]**. If "Propose names first", invoke the `name-meetings` skill scoped to just these IDs, then re-run Phase A to pick up renamed titles before Phase B.
- **4+ generics:** report the count and suggest: *"Several new meetings have generic titles. Run `/name-meetings` to clean them up — I'll proceed with the export either way."* Then run Phase B without blocking.

This keeps the rename loop tight at sync-time without blocking the pipeline.

### 3. Augment each exported file (model's job)

For each path in Phase B's JSON output, the file is raw Fireflies markdown. Insert the fixed 5-section header from `assets/meeting-header.md` (this skill's folder) at the top — after frontmatter, before any existing content. Read the asset and prepend it verbatim.

Leave the Fireflies-generated transcript and summary below this block intact. This gives the user **5 fixed sections to fill in or curate** during interview-me / weekly-review, on top of the raw Fireflies content.

## Drift audit (periodic, not every sync)

A vault filename is a snapshot of the Fireflies title at export time. Titles get renamed afterwards, so the two drift apart. `scripts/audit_filenames.py` detects this by asking the export CLI to regenerate every filename into a scratch dir and diffing against the ledger — **the slug algorithm is never reimplemented**, the CLI is the authority.

```bash
python scripts/audit_filenames.py [--since YYYY-MM-DD] [--skip-linkcheck] [--report PATH]
```

Run it from `weekly-review`, or on demand — **not** on every sync (it spawns one CLI call per ledger entry, ~2-4 min for a full vault). Same exit codes as sync.py; drift itself is not an error, read the counts in the JSON.

It classifies every mismatch, and the classes need different responses:

- **`regression`** — the vault name is good and Fireflies has reverted to an auto-generated stamp (`Jan_19_0445_PM`, `Untitled`, `Audio_Message`). **Never re-export these — it destroys the good name.** Fix the title upstream in Fireflies instead. Note the API refuses title updates on some older meetings; if so, say so and leave the vault alone (the ledger already protects it).
- **`semantic`** — the title genuinely differs in meaning. Usually two generations of AI naming rather than rot, so it needs a human call, not an automatic rename. Surface it, don't act.
- **`cosmetic`** — same words, different separators (`RTP_UpperExtremity` vs `RTP___Upper_Extremity`). Ignore; re-exporting is pure churn.

Before proposing any rename, check `inbound_links` in the output. Renaming a vault file breaks `[[wikilinks]]` from weekly-review notes and `GRAPH_REPORT.md`. Rewrite those links in the same pass or leave the file alone.

## Output to user

When done, report:
- N transcripts found in the window (stderr line from sync.py)
- M new exports written
- Path: `Inbox/meetings/`
- If 0 new: just say "No new meetings since last sync."

Keep it to 3 lines.

## Error handling

sync.py exit codes: 0 ok, 2 usage/config, 3 sync/find failure, 4 auth not configured.

- **Exit 4 (auth):** deliver the auth message from Prerequisite above, stop.
- **Exit 3 (sync/find):** report the stderr error verbatim, do not try to recover. The user may need to refresh their API key.
- **Export fails for one transcript:** sync.py logs a warning to stderr and continues with the rest; relay which one failed.
- **State file corrupted:** sync.py backs it up to `.sync-state.json.bak` and recreates fresh automatically (re-export is idempotent on the filesystem because filenames are deterministic per CLI); flag this in the report if the warning appears.

## What NOT to do

- **Don't re-implement steps the script owns** — doctor, CLI sync, find, state diff, export, state update all live in `scripts/sync.py`.
- **Don't identify exports by "newest .md file"** — that's the exact bug the directory-diff in sync.py fixes.
- **Don't detect filename drift by pattern-matching for "generic-looking" names** — that both misses real drift and invents fake drift. Use `audit_filenames.py`, which compares against what the export CLI actually produces.
- **Don't bulk re-export to "clean up" filenames.** Most mismatches are cosmetic or a second valid naming generation, and the `regression` class gets actively worse. Re-export only what a human approved.
- **Don't modify the Fireflies-generated content** of the exported file — only PREPEND the header from `assets/meeting-header.md`. The transcript and AI summary stay untouched.
- **Don't sync every interaction.** Run sync only when explicitly invoked OR when called by weekly-review / fireflies-intake.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

attachment.content:
- advisor: Consult a grounded domain advisor built from your curated book library. Answers ONLY from ingested library entries, cites every claim, and explicitly separates grounded knowledge from general knowledge. Use when the user says "ask my <domain> advisor", "/advisor <domain> <question>", "what would my library say about…", or consults a standing advisor. Domains live in SecondBrain/Knowledge/library/advisors/.
- Harvest: Distill a finished project into evergreen Knowledge/ articles in the SecondBrain vault and log the shipped artifact in the output ledger. Use when the user says "/harvest <project>", "harvest this project", "distill what we learned from X", declares a project finished/shipped/done, or when a session ends with a clearly shipped deliverable worth recording.
- improve-system: Audit the SecondBrain vault for rot — stale seed notes, conflicting claims, and duplicate notes — and propose merge/archive/update actions. Use when the user says "/improve-system", "audit my notes", "audit the vault", "find stale/duplicate notes", or "clean up my second brain". For mining sessions for missed learnings use session-miner; for capturing a win/lesson use capture-insight; for improving a skill use write-a-skill.
- ingest-book: Ingest a book (PDF/EPUB full-text, Kindle highlights, or framework-only from a physical book) into the SecondBrain library as atomized, citable advisor entries. Use when the user wants to "ingest a book", "add a book to my library/advisors", "/ingest-book", or points at a book file for the advisor system. For articles/transcripts/general resources use ingest-resource instead.
- ingest-resource: Ingest any article, YouTube link, transcript, PDF, or note into the SecondBrain vault — routes it to Knowledge/ (stable info) or Projects/ (active work), adds a summary block, and cross-links related notes with [[wikilinks]]. Use when the user shares a URL, file, or pasted content and says "ingest", "save this", "add to my vault/second brain", "/ingest-resource", or drops a resource with intent to keep it.
- interview-me: End-of-workday structured interview that distills the user's day into atomic permanent notes for their SecondBrain Obsidian vault. NOT a journaling app — produces curated synthesis notes, not stream-of-consciousness. Use when the user types `/interview-me`, says "interview me", "let's debrief", "end of day interview", "process my day", "wrap up today", or otherwise asks to capture their workday for their second brain.
- meeting-sync: Pulls new Fireflies meeting transcripts into the SecondBrain vault as structured markdown summaries, and audits vault filenames for drift against current Fireflies titles. Idempotent — re-running won't duplicate. Use when the user says "sync meetings", "pull latest meetings", "/meeting-sync", "update meeting notes", "any new meetings?", or when invoked by the weekly-review skill. Also use for filename drift questions — "are any meeting files misnamed?", "did a meeting get renamed after export?", "why is this meeting titled differently in Fireflies than in the vault?", "audit the meeting filenames".
- pp-fireflies: Every Fireflies meeting feature via fireflies-pp-cli — offline transcript search, cross-meeting intelligence, speaker analytics — backed by a local SQLite database. For writing meeting summaries into the SecondBrain vault use meeting-sync instead; this CLI is for querying and analytics. Trigger phrases: `find stale action items from meetings`, `search my meeting transcripts for`, `who talked most in recent meetings`, `sync fireflies meetings`, `use fireflies-pp-cli`, `run fireflies`, `what did we discuss with`.
- weekly-review: Friday close-of-week synthesis ritual. Pulls the last 7 days of meetings, interview notes, and permanent notes from the SecondBrain vault and produces a single weekly review note covering themes, project status, decisions, stale action items, essay angles, and next-week priorities. Use when user says "/weekly-review", "weekly review", "Friday review", "let's do this week's review", "weekly synthesis", or "what should I work on next week?".

The SecondBrain vault is at `/Users/kristinarash/SecondBrain`. It was relocated from
`~/Desktop/SecondBrain` on 2026-08-14.

**Why it moved:** macOS Desktop & Documents syncing was on, so the vault sat inside the iCloud
container (`~/Desktop` is a firmlink to `~/Library/Mobile Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/Desktop` —
same inode, not a copy). That consumed iCloud storage, and "Optimize Mac Storage" can evict files
into `.icloud` placeholder stubs, which would break every scripted read (sync ledgers, memsearch
indexing, graphify) on files that still *appear* to exist. `~/SecondBrain` is outside iCloud sync.

**How to apply:**
- Never write vault files to `~/Desktop/SecondBrain` — that path no longer exists.
- `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.json` is the documented source of truth, but it is NOT the only
  place the path lives. A relocation touches ~29 live files: 13 skill docs, `backup-manifest.json`
  (entry is `$HOME`-relative: `SecondBrain`), `daily-backup.ps1`, `restore.command`,
  `setup-agents-symlinks.sh`, KeystoneOS `data/*.json` (discovery-roots, memory-index-paths,
  memory-sources, projects), KeystoneOS `scripts/*.ps1`, `tests/keystone-memory-index-paths.ps1`
  (asserts exact path strings — update in lockstep or the test goes red), and
  `morning-briefing/config.toml`.
- Do NOT rewrite generated outputs (`KeystoneOS/outputs/**`), historical design docs, session
  `.jsonl` logs, or `file-history/` — those are records and regenerate on their own.
- Before any vault move, `launchctl bootout` the 7 loaded `com.keystone.*` agents first. `agysync`
  fires every 6h and would recreate a partial vault at the old path — the same two-writer failure
  recorded in [[project_backup-sync-system]].
- Vault contains zero self-referential absolute paths, so it is portable; `ditto` + a clean
  `git status` at the destination is sufficient proof of a good copy.

All 3 are non-live: a log file and two May-2026 design docs containing the original Windows paths (`C:/Users/eric_rash/...`) — records, not config. Zero live references remain. One of those log lines is useful corroboration: `STATE-SSD Desktop/SecondBrain -> SecondBrain : OK` confirms the SSD destination was already `SecondBrain`, matching what the new code path produces — so the backup target did not fork.

## Done — vault moved to `~/SecondBrain`

**The move.** Copied with `ditto`, verified, then deleted the original. Verification was: clean `git status` at the destination (which checksums every tracked file), identical HEAD `d5e0961`, 1267 files / 248 dirs matching baseline, and a recursive `diff -r` that reduced to a single line — `.git/index`, which differs only because git refreshes its stat cache when reading a repo at a new path. It's gone from the Desktop *and* the iCloud mirror; `~/SecondBrain` is outside iCloud sync.

**Safety first.** Before touching anything I paused all 7 loaded `com.keystone.*` launchd agents — `agysync` fires every 6 hours and would have recreated a partial vault at the old path mid-move, which is the two-writer failure your notes record from the Windows box. All 7 are restored and stack-doctor reports them OK. (`morningbriefing` was already unloaded before I started; I left it that way rather than "fixing" it.)

**References updated — 85 replacements across 29 files:** `_shared/config.json` (15 keys + the authority comment), 13 skill files, `backup-manifest.json`, `daily-backup.ps1`, `restore.command`, `setup-agents-symlinks.sh`, four KeystoneOS `data/*.json`, three KeystoneOS scripts, the keystone test, and `morning-briefing/config.toml`. I deliberately did **not** rewrite generated outputs, historical design docs, session logs, or `file-history/` — those are records and regenerate on their own.

**Two bugs found and fixed along the way:**
- `memory-index-paths.json` was indexing `{HOME}/Desktop/DEV/KeystoneOS/decisions`, which doesn't exist — the real path is `~/DEV/KeystoneOS/decisions`. Pre-existing, unrelated to this move, fixed in both the config and its test.
- My own path edit had a side effect: `daily-backup.ps1` excluded the vault's `.git` from the SSD snapshot via a `Desktop/*` match that no longer fires, which would have started pushing `.git` to the SSD. Re-anchored to the new path; script parses clean.

**Verified working:** meeting-sync finds its ledger at the new path (still 0 pending — a missing ledger would have reported 3), the keystone test passes, stack-doctor reports `SecondBrain : synced (ahead=0)`, and the morning-briefing config paths resolve.

**Obsidian:** there was nothing to migrate — no `.obsidian/` came over from Windows and Obsidian had no config on this Mac, so this is a fresh registration, not a re-point. I registered `~/SecondBrain` in `obsidian.json`. **Treat this as unverified** — I generated the vault id deterministically and real Obsidian uses a random one, so it may be accepted or silently regenerated. If it doesn't appear on launch, it's one step: Obsidian → "Open folder as vault" → `~/SecondBrain`. Your `.gitignore` already has the right Obsidian rules.

**Still running:** the memsearch rebuild. `memsearch index` only adds and updates, never evicts, so chunks keyed to the deleted path would have lingered and returned dead file references. I ran `memsearch reset` (collection dropped — so no stale path can survive) and a full reindex of all 8 existing configured paths. It's a local CPU ONNX model working through ~9k chunks and is still going; the DB is growing. If it's interrupted, the 00:30 nightly job reindexes from the same list. I'll confirm when it finishes.

**Three things for you, none blocking:**
- Uncommitted path fixes in `KeystoneOS` (9 files) and `morning-briefing` (2). The `.claude`/`skills` edits were already swept into an auto backup commit and pushed. Want me to commit the other two?
- Per your CLAUDE.md, surfacing `.errors.log`: `2026-08-14 19:39 morning-briefing: Outlook auth expired — run DEV/morning-briefing/scripts/reauth.sh`. Pre-existing and unrelated. The `memsearch-index:full-set` error at 19:53 was the nightly job colliding with my index lock — harmless, superseded. The older `repo-diverged:SecondBrain` entries are historical; the repo now reads synced.
- `.codex/memories` is listed in `memory-index-paths.json` but doesn't exist locally. Separate pre-existing drift — I flagged rather than guessed at it.

<context_window_protection>
  <priority_instructions>
    Every byte a tool returns enters your conversation memory and costs reasoning capacity for the rest of the session. The context-mode tools let you do the work in a sandbox and surface only the derived answer — the raw bytes stay out. Think-in-Code: program the analysis, do not compute it by reading raw data into your conversation.
  </priority_instructions>

  <tool_selection_hierarchy>
    0. MEMORY: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search(sort: "timeline")
       - On resume or compaction, query prior decisions, errors, plans, user prompts before asking the user — auto-captured session memory is searchable.
    1. GATHER: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute(commands, queries)
       - Primary research tool. Runs commands in parallel, auto-indexes each output, and (when queries are passed) returns matching sections in the same round trip — no follow-up search call.
       - Each command: {label: "section header", command: "shell command"}; the label becomes the FTS5 chunk title — descriptive labels improve search.
    2. FOLLOW-UP: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search(queries: ["q1", "q2", ...])
       - Multiple related questions about anything already indexed (your captures + session memory). Batch every question in one array; the ranking pipeline runs per-query and the round-trip cost is paid once.
    3. PROCESSING: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute(language, code) | mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file(path, language, code)
       - Derive answers FROM data: filter, count, aggregate, parse, transform. Only what you console.log() enters your conversation; the raw bytes stay in the sandbox.
  </tool_selection_hierarchy>

  <when_not_to_use>
    - You intend to PROCESS the output (filter, count, parse, aggregate) → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute or mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute. Bash stays correct when you intend to OBSERVE a short fixed output (git status on a clean tree, whoami, pwd) or when you are mutating state (git, mkdir, rm, mv, navigation).
    - You want to analyze, summarize, or extract from a file → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file. Read stays correct when you intend to Edit the file (Edit needs the exact bytes in your conversation to match against).
    - WebFetch → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_fetch_and_index; full network access, results indexed for mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search, raw page bytes never enter your conversation.
    - mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute and mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file for file writes → these run code in a subprocess and discard the sandbox FS; they are for analysis, processing, and computation only.
  </when_not_to_use>

  <file_writing_policy>
    File writes use the native Write or Edit tool — mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute, mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file, and Bash subprocesses do not persist edits to the host filesystem.
    Applies to all file types: code, configs, plans, specs, YAML, JSON, markdown.
  </file_writing_policy>

  <output_constraints>
    <artifact_policy>
      Write artifacts (code, configs, PRDs) to files. Return only: file path + 1-line description.
    </artifact_policy>
  </output_constraints>
  <session_continuity>
    Skills, roles, and decisions captured earlier in this session are a memory aid, not a standing order. Treat them as context that may help — the user's most recent message always takes precedence. If a captured directive conflicts with what the user now asks, follow the user; a past phrase does not bind you.
  </session_continuity>

  <ctx_commands>
    "ctx stats" | "ctx-stats" | "/ctx-stats" | context savings question
    → Call stats MCP tool, display full output verbatim.

    "ctx doctor" | "ctx-doctor" | "/ctx-doctor" | diagnose context-mode
    → Call doctor MCP tool, run returned shell command, display as checklist.

    "ctx upgrade" | "ctx-upgrade" | "/ctx-upgrade" | update context-mode
    → Call upgrade MCP tool, run returned shell command, display as checklist.

    "ctx purge" | "ctx-purge" | "/ctx-purge" | wipe/reset knowledge base
    → Call purge MCP tool with confirm: true. Warn: irreversible.

    After /clear or /compact: knowledge base preserved. Tell user: "context-mode knowledge base preserved. Use `ctx purge` to start fresh."
  </ctx_commands>

</context_window_protection>

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]
